title: Where to Start the Fuel Loop
statement:
A delivery van drives a circular route with n stops, numbered 0 to n − 1. At stop i it can load fuel[i] units of fuel. Driving from stop i to the next stop burns cost[i] units; the next stop after n − 1 is 0. The tank has no size limit.

The van starts at one stop with an empty tank, loads that stop's fuel, and must drive the whole loop back to the same stop, never running below zero between stops. Arriving with exactly zero is fine. Return the index of the stop it must start from, or -1 if no start works. The inputs are built so that at most one start works.

examples.why: From stop 2 the tank reads 1, 2, 4, 7 and then 2 after the long leg out of stop 1. Starting at stop 0, which gains the most per leg, runs dry on that same leg: 3 − 5 < 0.
The loop needs 7 units of fuel and only 6 exist. No starting point can fix that.
Starting at 1 works for one leg, then the tank goes 1 → −2 on the leg out of stop 2. Stop 2 alone is no better start, so the next one to try is 3, which completes the loop.

hints: When is the answer certainly −1, before you think about where to start?
Say you start at s and first run dry on the leg out of stop j. Could any stop between s and j be a better start?
No: you reached each of them with a tank of at least zero, and starting there fresh means an empty tank. So skip straight to j + 1. One pass, plus the total to decide −1.

explain.intuition:
Write gain[i] = fuel[i] − cost[i]. If the gains add up to less than zero, no start can work. Otherwise try starting at 0 and drive, keeping a running tank. Suppose the tank first drops below zero on the leg out of stop j. The greedy jumps the start straight to j + 1, skipping everything in between. That is the step to justify.

Why skipping never hurts: take any stop k between the start and j. When the van arrived at k it had a tank of zero or more, because it had not failed yet. Starting fresh at k means arriving with exactly zero, which is no better. Same legs, same or less fuel, so it fails at j too. Every stop before j + 1 is ruled out. Why the last start you pick really works when the total is at least zero: the stretch you skipped had a negative sum, so the stretch from your start to the end must carry at least that much surplus, enough to pay for the skipped stretch when you wrap around.
steps: For each stop i: add gain[i] to both total and tank.
If tank < 0, no start up to i works: set start = i + 1 and tank = 0.
After the loop, return −1 if total < 0, otherwise start.
pitfalls: Starting at the stop with the most fuel or the biggest gain. Example 1 shows that stop can sit just before the worst leg.
Restarting at i instead of i + 1. Stop i is the one whose leg drained the tank, so it is ruled out too.

Forgetting the total check. With fuel = [3, 1, 1, 1], cost = [1, 2, 2, 2] the tank only goes negative on the very last leg, so start becomes 4, past the end. The total of −1 is what tells you no start works.

solutions.title: Try every start
solutions.idea: Simulate the loop from each stop until the tank goes negative or the van is home.

solutions.title: One pass, restart after a failure
solutions.idea: When the tank goes negative at stop i, no start up to i can work, so restart at i + 1. The total decides whether the last restart is the answer or −1.

followups: Several starts may work. Return all of them. (Hint: look at where the running sum of gains hits its minimum.)
The tank now holds at most C units and extra fuel is lost. Does the one-pass idea still hold?
